dream: I stand at the centre of a vast circular courtyard where four coloured streams flow inward from opposite gates. Each carries anger, tenderness, ambition, and grief, and for a long time they clash without mixing. Then a quiet gold light rises from the stone beneath my feet. The opposing currents curve into one ring around me.

In a dark hall two versions of myself sit at opposite ends of a long table, each insisting the other must leave. Neither yields. A third presence waits in the room without choosing sides. When I stop trying to banish either figure, the table splits open into a spiral stair that descends and ascends at once.

A neighbour I have always praised for patience appears at my door covered in mud, laughing with a cruelty I have never allowed myself. He lists every petty resentment I have edited out of my speech and dares me to deny him. I try to shut the door, but his voice keeps speaking from inside my own mouth.

I chase a thief through alleys and catch him in a dead end, only to see my own face under his hood. He carries away qualities I refused at work: blunt honesty, raw desire, the appetite to win. When I condemn him, the alley walls narrow. When I reach toward him, he remains dangerous, yet unmistakably mine.

Backstage before a lecture, I discover my suit has been stitched directly to my skin along the seams. Each time I practice the polished opening I wrote for the audience, the fabric tightens, and a softer sentence dies in my throat. In the mirror I see two faces layered: the competent speaker the hall expects, and a tired private face pressed beneath the collar.

At a family reunion I wear a name tag with a title that is not quite mine—slightly too formal, slightly too accomplished. Relatives praise the title while asking questions my real life cannot answer. Every polite adjustment I make alters how much space I am allowed at the table. When I remove the badge, people still respond to the performance as though it were my face.

A woman made of river-light stands between me and a door I have tried to force open by effort alone. She tilts her head toward the hinge side I ignored, and my urgency loosens. When I listen, the door breathes open a crack. When I grab the knob, she dims but does not leave.

I walk a shoreline at dusk beside a stranger whose presence makes the landscape more vivid. She redirects every choice—whether to wade in, whether to turn back—by the quality of her attention. Without her, the sea is flat grey. With her beside me, the water darkens into something I want to enter.

On a bare ridge a man in a worn coat speaks only in clear, impersonal truths that cut through my excuses without insult. When I argue for comfort, he points to a narrow descent I had labelled impossible. He neither flatters nor threatens; he simply waits until I start walking toward the path he indicated.

In a library of locked cases, a figure keeps placing the correct key just out of my reach until I state what I am actually willing to stand for. Each declaration rearranges the shelves, and books I never noticed step forward. When I finally speak without hedging, the lock opens to a corridor that was not on any floor plan.

During a city blackout an infant in my arms remains calmly luminous while adults panic in the streets below. When officials demand I hand the child over for safekeeping, I refuse and climb the stairwell. Sirens fade as we reach rooms above the roofline filled with daylight that had been unavailable all evening.

A small child walks into the centre of a courtroom where rigid old verdicts repeat on loop and touches the judge’s gavel. The room cannot proceed in the former way; cases dissolve and re-form. Clerks stare at dockets rewriting themselves in handwriting none of them trained to use.

Lost in winter hills, I follow warmth to a woman kneading bread beside a door that opens into a greenhouse flooded with spring. She wraps a blanket around me without questions, and my frozen hands regain colour. Steam from the oven loosens the ache in my chest, and seedlings inside the glass lean toward her palms.

I drift in dark water until a vast figure gathers me into an embrace that is ocean and cradle at once. She sings a low tone that aligns my breathing with tides, and broken things inside me surface to be tended. Kelp braids around us like a soft fence. When I try to cling in fear, she loosens just enough that I must swim on my own.

My mother fills every doorway of the house with soft blankets and steaming bowls, smiling as she explains I am still too fragile to go out. Each attempt to leave adds another loving lock. Keys appear in her apron pocket for my own good, and windows fog so thoroughly I cannot see the street.

In a garden that should be mine, an older woman uproots every plant I set in the earth and replants it closer to her porch, humming lullabies. She insists this is protection while the roots strangle in crowded soil. When I protest, she weeps until guilt reverses my steps, then feeds me sweet cake as reward for staying near her chair.

In a cherry orchard at harvest I climb for fruit while my father’s voice fills the phone and then the whole field. He demands I answer now, that my day belongs to his schedule, and when I hesitate he shouts until the branches shake. Though he is not standing beside me, his claim occupies the hour I had set aside for picking.

My father storms through my flat demanding I report every plan for the week. When I refuse, he raises a fist of pure authority—then cousins arrive and he softens into sweetness, calling me darling and asking for a greeting. The sweetness traps my anger so I cannot keep the boundary I had begun to form.

At a mountain pass where three trails look identical, an old man with ash on his sleeves draws one line in the snow that reveals a fourth trail hidden by perspective. He speaks little. Ravens above us circle once and fly toward the line he drew. After he turns away, the path he indicated remains in the snow.

Inside a ruined observatory, an elder astronomer hands me a lens cracked in a deliberate pattern. Through it, constellations rearrange into a story about my life I had misread as random crisis. Dust motes in the dome drift into the same shape after he speaks. He points to a cluster I had always avoided as merely empty sky.

An old woman in a red shawl sits at a crossroads spinning thread from nettles without gloves. She tells me which strand will cut and which will bind. When I reach for the easy thread, she redirects my hand to the rough one. Spindle wounds on her fingers gleam like small stars.

Deep in a root cellar, a crone sorts seeds by moon phases and presses one into my palm with instructions not to plant it until I name what must die. The seed warms when I speak honestly, and the cellar walls sketch a map of the next year in frost and soot. Mice pause in their routes to listen.

I cross a bridge of black ice spanning a gorge where a wounded animal waits on the far side. Each step cracks under me, and wind tries to slide me into the ravine, but I keep moving until I reach the creature and carry it back. The return path rises instead of falling. When I set the animal down, the dry wells roar alive.

Guards block a citadel gate at dawn, and I challenge their captain to single combat to win passage for refugees behind me. The fight drains me, yet when the captain yields, the gates open onto a road we were told was myth. Families stream through before the sun fully rises. My body is scarred, but the crossing is real.

At a tribunal I am accused using forged letters I never wrote. Instead of defending my innocence straight on, I laugh and forge the judge’s signature in plain sight, swapping the charges onto the accuser’s own ledger. Corrupt officials flee through a door that appeared only after the reversal. Townspeople outside cheer as the record now indicts the bench itself.

A merchant insists I pay twice for a bridge I already crossed. I pretend to agree, hide coins in a hollow boot, and let him discover payment that makes his scales declare him debtor to the town. He chases me, but the townspeople now bar his tollhouse with new rules he cannot read without admitting fraud. Children cross freely for the first time in years.

A hooded ferryman meets me at a river that smells of iron and lilies. He adjusts my footing in the boat each time I reach for the wrong shore. Midstream the sky folds, and we arrive in a grey city where clocks run backward and my breath fogs in summer heat.

At the mouth of a cave that breathes cold air, a lantern-bearer walks half a step ahead, never touching me yet preventing each misstep into the drop. Inside, tunnels split into memories that are not mine, then reunite in a chamber where gravity loosens. When I hesitate, she marks the stone with a symbol that makes the return path visible even when I close my eyes.

On the morning of my promotion, a colleague enters wearing my clothes, speaking my anecdotes, and receiving congratulations meant for me. When I protest, the room looks through me as if I were the copy. HR calls his name using mine, and my desk keys no longer fit the lock that bears my photograph.

I audition for a role I trained years to play, but the director pairs me with an understudy who mirrors my blocking exactly one beat ahead. Each time I innovate, he executes the move first and receives the note of praise. The cast begins blocking me from the stage entrance as though I were the intruder.

I wander a station where every departure board flickers to cities I cannot name, clutching a ticket no window will honour. People embrace under clocks while I stand in the empty centre, unclaimed. Announcements call names that are almost mine but never quite match my mouth. Each attempt to join a crowd dissolves at the edge.

After a flood, I search ruined streets calling for family and hear only my voice echo from empty houses. A neighbour offers spare blankets but no place at the table that was once shared. I sleep in porches and hide from officials who ask for names tied to lineages I no longer have. Photographs peel from walls and curl in water without showing faces I recognize.

In a candlelit hall I choose to walk toward one person while another suitable match waits politely aside. The chosen one and I speak without scripts, and the room narrows to pulse and breath until a vow forms. When we touch, alliances in the background shift. Even servants change allegiance before the music ends.

Separated by a glass wall from someone I love, I press both palms forward until the barrier warms and cracks along the shape of our hands. Neither of us looks away. Others warn of ruin, but we keep pressing. Shards fall inward without cutting us, and the air on both sides finally smells the same.

I enter a hall where no ceremony is in progress yet every dispute halts when I sit on the stone seat at the far wall. My judgments are few, but each reorders resources—water routed to dry fields, guards withdrawn from a border provocation. Petitioners leave before speaking twice, as though my will has already entered their plans.

During a siege I stand on the ramparts as the one whose word releases or withholds the gates. Envoys appeal to law, but I must choose whether to endure starvation or open trade. When I speak, banners change colour along the walls. Messengers repeat my sentence before I finish it, and the crowd below waits.

I am buried in wet earth still breathing, feeling old ambitions dissolve into silence. Roots pass through my ribs without pain, and seasons compress above me—snow, rain, drought—until a green shoot pushes out through my sternum into open air. I climb out stripped of former roles, unable to speak the old language but able to walk.

A moth-wing cloak burns away on my shoulders while I walk through a night market, and strangers mourn the fabric though I feel lighter. At the river I wade until the current pulls me under; downstream I emerge with new skin and a laugh that startles me. Vendors who knew my old face bow to someone they cannot name.

In a domed chamber, a bright figure and a dark figure stand apart on opposite mosaic hemispheres. When they join hands, the floor becomes a third symbol neither could form alone—a living mandala that breathes. Priests at the rim fall silent as the new pattern pulses through the walls.

I carry a bowl of water and my counterpart carries fire; we are told only one element may enter the shrine. At the threshold we pour and kindle together, and steam rises into a bird that circles once and settles on both our shoulders. The priests step back because the altar opens without their formula.

A beloved stranger meets me at a cliff edge where the path has vanished and takes my hand. We descend a stair that appears step by step only while we maintain contact, passing through layers of air that feel like different decades of my life.

A hooded guide leads me into a tomb where my former name is carved on the lid. Inside I lie down willingly, shed skin like a brittle coat, and rise while he steadies my first breath in the upper world. Torches mark each turn of the passage, and the air changes weight as we cross from burial chamber to dawn slope.

A man who looks like me mocks my careful reputation in front of colleagues, exposing lies I told to stay respectable. Instead of crushing him, I join his ridicule and swap the meeting agenda for truths that shatter a false hierarchy. Laughter turns into strategy when I forge new minutes that redistribute authority to those silenced.

I am crowned in public while the part of me that still wears yesterday’s clothes watches from behind the curtain. I step forward and accept command, then immediately perform a role that reshapes how the court treats me. Decrees leave my mouth in a voice trained for ceremony, yet each order reorganises real resources in the kingdom below.

She appears first as a distant figure on a balcony who makes the city feel inhabited, then later beside me in rain that erases street signs. I choose her over a safer match endorsed by friends. My chest loosens, and the chosen bond reshapes who waits for me at the corner.

To retrieve medicine for my village I descend a volcano’s throat, lose armour layer by layer to heat, and crawl back out carrying the vial in bare hands. I return altered—voice rougher, priorities simplified. Elders who sent me do not recognize my gait until I speak a vow I could not have uttered before the descent.

Opposite forces within me personify as sun and moon avatars who refuse truce until I hold both wrists at the centre of a wheel. When they touch, the wheel becomes a single luminous face that is also the room. The ceiling fills with a pattern I feel in my bones, and opposing temperaments fuse into a third order that governs the space.

Cold and unclaimed on a platform, I am found by a vast presence who wraps me and feeds me without asking pedigree. For the first time I stop searching ticket counters, yet I cling tightly from habit. Warm bread steam and blanket weight settle over me while the ache of prior emptiness still hums beneath.

A queen-mother rules the citadel with velvet decrees that forbid anyone to leave her table while she smiles. Servants set extra plates for guests who never arrive, and the doors seal whenever someone reaches for the hall. Courtiers obey from fear of her withdrawal of care.

An old man meets me at a forest edge, explains the meaning of the three paths, then walks the middle one beside me as the trees shift into an underworld grove. Roots glow faintly where he steps, marking a route I could not see from the treeline alone.

My duplicate sits in my chair at dinner, wearing my name tag, while I stand unseen in the corner. When I finally confront him, he speaks every cruel truth I suppress and refuses to yield the seat. Guests defer to him as host, and my plate is cleared before I touch it.

I unload groceries in a familiar kitchen, rinse vegetables, and argue mildly with myself about whether to cook pasta or rice. The tap drips in a rhythm I have heard for years. The refrigerator light behaves exactly as it does when I am awake.

I push a massive stone up a long hill toward a gate that never arrives closer. My muscles burn, sweat blinds me, and the stone rolls back each time I near what looks like the top. Dawn comes and goes, and my hands bleed in the same grooves they occupied at the start.

A stern guard stands before a bridge and checks passports without looking up. I ask which way leads to the other shore, and he repeats that passage requires valid papers. When the bell tolls, he simply closes the gate. Travelers behind me turn back, and the river keeps flowing beneath locked chains.

I descend a staircase into a cold basement where a coffin lies open under a single bulb. The air smells of clay and old flowers; I touch the lid and feel only the finality of weight. Moths circle the bulb without changing it, and the stairs above remain exactly as I left them.

A salesman promises delivery of a machine that never arrives, changing dates each call. I feel foolish and angry. My neighbours shrug and say I should have known better, and the shop window stays dark through every rescheduled week he invents.

At work I answer emails and attend a stand-up meeting where everyone reports tasks. I wear a lanyard because building policy requires it. After lunch I return to the same desk and the same mild fatigue.

A storm blows shingles off the roof and water stains spread across the ceiling. I move buckets and call a repair service. Insurance forms, wet towels, and the contractor’s ladder fill the scene from start to finish.
I repaint a bedroom from blue to yellow, rearrange furniture, and feel briefly refreshed. I sleep in the new colour and wake with the same unfinished letter on the nightstand.

A friend on the phone lists sensible steps for my job search—update the resume, network, apply broadly, follow up politely. We hang up and I make tea, the conversation already fading before the kettle boils.

I babysit a neighbour’s toddler who spills juice and cries for his mother. I comfort him until she returns. The sticky floor remains a chore, and once the door closes the apartment returns to adult quiet exactly as before he arrived.

Βρισκόμουν σε έναν τεράστιο υπόγειο σταθμό, αλλά αντί για τρένα υπήρχε ένα μαύρο ποτάμι. Η σύντροφός μου είχε χαθεί πίσω από μια σιδερένια πύλη στην άλλη όχθη. Ένας σιωπηλός βαρκάρης αρνήθηκε να με περάσει, ώσπου έβγαλα ένα μικρό βιολί και έπαιξα. Τότε άνοιξε τη βάρκα και με πέρασε απέναντι. Βρήκα τη σύντροφό μου και μια φωνή μάς είπε ότι μπορούσαμε να επιστρέψουμε, αρκεί να μη γυρίσω να την κοιτάξω πριν φτάσουμε στο φως. Άκουγα τα βήματά της πίσω μου σε όλη τη διαδρομή. Λίγο πριν από την έξοδο σταμάτησα να τα ακούω. Γύρισα από φόβο και την είδα να τραβιέται πάλι πίσω από την πύλη, ενώ εγώ έμενα μόνος στο φως.

Ήμουν σε ένα μεγάλο θέατρο όπου όλοι περίμεναν να παρουσιάσω τα οικονομικά μιας εταιρείας. Πριν βγω στη σκηνή, μου φόρεσαν μια τέλεια σκούρα στολή με το όνομά μου κεντημένο στο στήθος. Μόλις στάθηκα μπροστά στο κοινό, η φωνή μου έγινε ψυχρή και επίσημη, παρότι μέσα μου ήθελα να πω ότι δεν γνώριζα τις απαντήσεις. Κάθε φορά που προσπαθούσα να μιλήσω με τη δική μου φωνή, ο γιακάς έσφιγγε και το κοινό σταματούσε να με βλέπει. Όταν επέστρεψα στα παρασκήνια, προσπάθησα να βγάλω τη στολή, αλλά τα μανίκια είχαν κολλήσει πάνω μου. Ξύπνησα την ώρα που έσκιζα προσεκτικά μία ραφή για να μπορέσω να αναπνεύσω.

Βρισκόμουν σε έναν γυμνό λόφο και έσπρωχνα μια τεράστια στρογγυλή πέτρα προς την κορυφή. Δεν υπήρχε κανείς να με παρακολουθεί και δεν ένιωθα ούτε γενναίος ούτε φοβισμένος· μόνο ήξερα ότι έπρεπε να τη φτάσω πάνω. Κάθε φορά που η πέτρα πλησίαζε στην κορυφή, ακουγόταν ένα μικρό κουδούνι και η πέτρα γλιστρούσε από τα χέρια μου, κυλούσε μέχρι κάτω και σταματούσε ακριβώς στο ίδιο σημείο. Κατέβαινα, έβαζα πάλι τα χέρια μου πάνω της και ξεκινούσα από την αρχή. Ξύπνησα λίγο πριν την σπρώξω για ακόμη μία φορά.

Ήμουν στην κουζίνα μου και ήθελα να πιω νερό. Άνοιξα το ντουλάπι, αλλά όλα τα ποτήρια ήταν άπλυτα. Πήρα το λιγότερο βρώμικο, το έπλυνα με σαπούνι, το ξέβγαλα δύο φορές και το γέμισα από τη βρύση. Η γάτα πέρασε από τον πάγκο και έριξε ένα κουταλάκι στο πάτωμα. Το σήκωσα, ήπια το νερό και ξύπνησα ελαφρώς εκνευρισμένος επειδή θυμήθηκα ότι είχα αφήσει πιάτα στον νεροχύτη.

Κατέβαινα σε ένα υπόγειο παλάτι περνώντας από επτά διαδοχικές πόρτες. Σε κάθε πόρτα ένας φύλακας μου ζητούσε να αφήσω κάτι: πρώτα το δαχτυλίδι μου, μετά το παλτό, τα παπούτσια, μια κάρτα με το όνομά μου, το περιδέραιο, τη ζώνη και τέλος ένα μικρό στέμμα που δεν ήξερα ότι φορούσα. Στην τελευταία αίθουσα στεκόταν μια σιωπηλή βασίλισσα. Με κοίταξε χωρίς να μιλήσει και έπεσα στο πάτωμα σαν να είχε φύγει όλη η ζωή από μέσα μου. Αργότερα δύο μικρές μορφές έριξαν νερό στο πρόσωπό μου και ξύπνησα μέσα στο όνειρο. Ανέβηκα ξανά από τις επτά πόρτες, αλλά δεν μπορούσα να πάρω πίσω όλα όσα είχα αφήσει. Βγήκα στην επιφάνεια φορώντας μόνο ένα απλό λευκό κορδόνι στον καρπό.
Elevator opens on the wrong floor. Grey corridor. No numbers. Door shuts before I step out.
Teeth loosen one by one into my palm. I spit into the sink. They are just teeth. The mirror stays ordinary.
A man with my face chases me through parking garages. I turn a corner and lose him. My reflection waits at the car window.
Someone I lost finds me at a bus stop in light rain. We stand close without speaking. The bus arrives but neither of us boards.

An old woman at a crossroads points down three paths without naming them. I ask which leads home; she shrugs and hands me a folded map I cannot open. Traffic sounds fade. I stand holding the paper while the roads look equally worn.

Water rises in a basement where I stored old boxes. I wade out through a side door into morning sunlight on wet grass. The house behind me looks the same from outside, but my clothes are dry and the street sounds sharper than I remember.
I float peacefully on a sea mattress while my boyfriend lies close above me. Together we look down into the water and explore the seabed below us. The whole scene stays calm, beautiful, and safe.

I ride the commuter train to the office, check two emails, and eat a sandwich at my desk. A colleague asks about a meeting time. I confirm three o’clock and save a spreadsheet. The afternoon passes without anything unusual happening.
